title: Below the Cortex
subtitle: Subcortical systems shape the whole brain
learningObjectives: Identify major subcortical systems relevant to cognition, affect, movement and homeostasis.
Explain cortico-subcortical loops rather than treating deep nuclei as isolated modules.
Relate subcortical dysfunction to cognitive, behavioural and autonomic presentations.

sections.explainSimply: Important structures sit deep inside the brain. They help control movement, memory, emotion, motivation and body regulation.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: The thalamus coordinates information flow; basal ganglia support action selection and habit; hippocampal systems support memory; hypothalamus regulates homeostasis; amygdala contributes to salience and threat learning.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical loops and limbic circuits integrate cognition, affect, motor control and reinforcement. Subcortical structures are heterogeneous nuclei, not unitary emotion modules.
sections.thinkOfItLike: The city’s transport hub, security network, archive and utilities department operating beneath the visible skyline.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Subcortical dysfunction can mimic “purely psychological” problems through apathy, impulsivity, memory change, sleep disruption or altered emotional learning.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Degeneration, hypoxia, inflammation and focal injury may disrupt movement, memory, motivation or autonomic regulation.
sections.clinicalPearl: Deep structures influence cortical processing continuously; “higher” does not mean independent.
sections.practicalExample: Disruption of frontostriatal circuits can produce slowed initiation, reduced cognitive flexibility or apathy even when primary cortical sensory and motor systems remain relatively intact.
sections.limitationsCautions: Terms such as “limbic system” and “basal ganglia” group heterogeneous structures. Clinical reasoning should specify nuclei, pathways and network context where possible.

quizBank.question: Which structure is central to forming new episodic memories?
quizBank.explanation: The hippocampal formation is crucial for encoding and consolidating new episodic memories.
